Football
soccer
the world game
Two teams of 11 try to send the ball into the other goal.
You may kick the ball or touch it with any part of the body except your hands and arms.
Only the goalkeeper may use hands, and only inside the penalty box.
A referee watches the rules. The game has two halves.
A goal scores one point. The whole ball must cross the line between the posts.
The team with more goals wins. If the score is level, the game can be a draw, or some matches use extra time.
On a grass or turf pitch, in almost every country.
Football is the world game. Some people call it soccer. The World Cup is played every four years.
A goal scores one point
On a grass pitch
Basketball
Two teams of five try to throw the ball through the other hoop.
You bounce the ball as you move. That is called a dribble.
You may pass the ball, or shoot it.
A referee watches the rules. The game is played in timed quarters.
A shot can score one, two, or three points. A free throw is one point.
The team with more points when time runs out wins.
On a court indoors, or on an outdoor playground.
The hoop is 10 feet high. That is about 3 metres.
Shots score 1, 2, or 3 points
On a hoop court
Cricket
One side bowls. The other side bats.
The bowler sends the ball toward the stumps. The batter tries to hit it.
Batters run between the wickets to score.
When ten batters are out, the innings ends.
You score runs by running, or by hitting the ball to the boundary. A boundary along the ground is four. Over the rope on the full is six.
The side with more runs wins the match.
On a large grass field, with a pitch in the middle.
A Test match can last up to five days.
You score runs
On a cricket field
Tennis
Players hit a ball over a net with a racquet.
The ball must land in the court.
You serve to start each point.
A match is played as singles or doubles.
Points make a game. Games make a set. Sets make the match.
The first player to win the needed sets wins the match.
On a clay, grass, or hard court.
Zero points in tennis is called love.
You score points, then games, then sets
On a tennis court
Athletics
track and field
track
Runners stay in their lane when the race asks them to.
Jumpers and throwers each get a set of tries.
A false start can cost you the race.
Judges watch the finish line and the measurements.
In a race, the clock and the finish order matter. In a jump or throw, the distance is measured.
In a race, first across the line wins. In a jump or throw, the best distance wins.
On a track, a field, or a road.
A marathon is 26.2 miles. That is about 42 kilometres.
First across the line, or the best distance
On a track or field
Swimming
You race in a lane.
Each stroke has its own rules. Freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, and butterfly are the main ones.
You must touch the wall at each turn.
You start when the starter says go.
The clock times your swim. First to touch the wall is ahead.
The first swimmer to touch the wall wins the race.
In a pool. Some races are in open water.
An Olympic pool is 50 metres long.
First to touch the wall
In a swimming pool
Gymnastics
You perform a routine on a set apparatus.
Artistic gymnastics uses floor, vault, bars, beam, rings, and pommel horse.
You must stay within the rules for your event.
Judges watch the whole routine.
Judges give a score for difficulty and for how well you perform.
The gymnast with the higher score wins.
In a gym, on mats and apparatus.
The balance beam is only 10 centimetres wide.
Judges score the routine
In a gym
Rugby union
rugby
Two teams of 15 try to move the oval ball up the pitch.
You may run with the ball, pass it backwards, or kick it.
A tackled player must release the ball.
A referee watches the rules.
A try is five points. A kick through the posts after a try adds two. A penalty kick is three.
The team with more points at the end wins.
On a grass pitch.
The Rugby World Cup is held every four years. Rugby sevens, a shorter game, is the one at the Olympic Games.
A try is five points
On a rugby pitch
American football
gridiron
nfl
Two teams of 11 try to move an oval ball toward the end zone.
You may run with the ball or throw it forward.
The team with the ball has four downs to gain 10 yards.
A touchdown is six points. A kick after it can add one. A field goal is three.
On a long field with yard lines.
The playing field is 100 yards long between the end zones.
A touchdown is six points
On a long gridiron
Baseball
One team pitches and fields. The other team bats.
The pitcher throws the ball. The batter tries to hit it.
Batters run to first, second, third, and home.
Each team bats in innings. A full game has nine innings.
You score a run when you touch every base and get home.
The team with more runs after nine innings wins. Extra innings are used if the score is level.
On a diamond of dirt and grass.
A home run means the ball goes over the outfield fence in fair ground.
On a baseball diamond
Volleyball
Two teams of six hit a ball over a net.
You may use your hands and arms. You may not catch the ball.
A team may touch the ball three times before it goes back over.
The same player may not hit it twice in a row.
You win a rally point when the other team cannot return the ball.
A set usually goes to 25 points, and you must lead by two. The first team to win three sets wins the match.
On an indoor court with a high net.
The net is higher for adults than for children.
Rally points go to 25
On an indoor court
Table tennis
ping pong
ping-pong
Players hit a small ball over a low net on a table.
You use a small bat.
The serve must bounce on your side, then the other side.
The ball must bounce once on the other side of the table.
You win a point when the other player misses the ball.
The first to 11 points wins the game, but you must lead by two.
On a table, indoors.
The ball is hollow and very light. A fast rally can last only a few seconds.
First to 11 points, and lead by two
On a table
Badminton
Players hit a shuttlecock over a high net with a racquet.
The shuttle must land in the court.
You serve underarm.
You play singles or doubles.
You win a point on each rally.
The first to 21 points wins the game, but you must lead by two. A match is usually best of three games.
On an indoor court.
A shuttlecock has a cone of feathers, or a plastic skirt.
First to 21 points, and lead by two
On a badminton court
Golf
You hit a small ball with a club toward a hole.
You play the ball where it lies.
You start each hole from the tee.
The ball must drop into the hole to finish it.
Each swing is one stroke. You count every stroke.
The player who finishes the holes in the fewest strokes wins.
On a golf course of fairways, rough, and greens.
A hole-in-one means the ball goes in the hole in one stroke.
The fewest strokes win
On a golf course
Cycling
Riders race on bikes.
You must follow the course.
In a track race, you stay inside the rules for the sprint or the chase.
A road race can be one long day, or many days.
In many races, the clock and the finish order matter. Some races also give points along the way.
In a road race or a sprint, first across the line wins.
On a road, a velodrome, or a mountain trail.
A peloton is the main group of riders packed together.
First across the line
On a road or a track
Boxing
Two boxers compete in a ring for timed rounds.
They wear gloves and head guards in many youth and Olympic bouts.
A referee watches the rules and can pause the bout.
Judges watch the whole bout.
Judges give points for clean scoring skills. The boxer with more points can win.
The boxer with the higher score wins the bout. A referee keeps it fair.
In a boxing ring.
Olympic boxing is scored by judges, round by round.
Judges give points
In a boxing ring
Wrestling
Two wrestlers compete on a mat.
You try to control the other wrestler within the rules.
Freestyle and Greco-Roman are two Olympic styles.
A referee watches every hold.
You score points for fair holds and for control on the mat.
The wrestler with more points when time ends wins. A very strong hold can end the match sooner.
On a wrestling mat.
Greco-Roman wrestlers may not grab below the waist. Freestyle wrestlers may.
A fair hold scores points
On a wrestling mat
Judo
Two judoka wear a strong jacket and belt.
You try to throw, hold, or control your partner within the rules.
You bow before the match.
A referee awards the scores.
A big clean throw can win at once. Smaller throws and holds give lower scores.
The judoka with the higher score wins. One perfect throw, called ippon, wins the match at once.
On a judo mat called a tatami.
Belt colours show how long a judoka has trained. Black belt is a high rank.
Throws and holds score points
On a judo mat
Taekwondo
Two athletes compete on a mat for timed rounds.
They wear a chest guard, a helmet, and foot pads.
Points land on the scoring pads.
Electronic pads help count the points. Clean scoring skills on the pads count. Higher skills can score more.
The person with more points wins.
On a taekwondo mat.
Taekwondo began in Korea. Athletes wear a chest guard and a helmet.
Hits on the pads score points
On a taekwondo mat
Fencing
Two fencers try to touch with a foil, an epee, or a sabre.
They wear a mask and a white jacket.
The piste is a long narrow strip.
A light shows when a touch is scored.
A point is scored when a touch lands on the target area.
The fencer with more points wins the bout.
On a fencing piste, indoors.
Foil, epee, and sabre each have a different target area.
A touch on the target scores a point
On a fencing piste
Archery
You shoot arrows at a round target.
You stand on the shooting line.
You wait for the signal before you shoot.
Judges check each arrow.
Arrows closer to the centre score more points. The gold centre is the top score.
The archer with the higher score wins.
At an archery range, outdoors or indoors.
The centre of the target is called the gold.
Arrows nearer the centre score more
At an archery range
Rowing
A crew races in a long narrow boat.
Rowers sit facing backwards and pull oars.
Each boat stays in its lane.
You must finish the set distance.
The clock times the boat. Lanes keep the race fair.
The first boat to cross the line wins.
On a calm river, a lake, or a rowing basin.
An Olympic rowing race is 2,000 metres.
The first boat across the line
On a river or a lake
Canoeing
kayak
Paddlers race in a canoe or a kayak.
In a sprint, you stay in a lane on calm water.
In slalom, you pass through gates on moving water.
You must paddle the whole course.
Sprint races use the clock. Slalom adds time for a missed gate.
In a sprint, first across the line wins. In slalom, the fastest fair time wins.
On a lake, a basin, or a white-water course.
In a kayak you sit low and use a paddle with two blades. In a canoe the paddle often has one blade.
First across the line, or the fastest time
On calm or wild water
Sailing
Boats race around marks on the water.
The wind pushes the sails.
You must leave each mark on the right side.
Right of way rules stop boats from bumping.
The first boats earn the best race scores. A series adds those scores up.
The boat with the best score across the races wins. In one race, first to finish within the rules wins.
On the sea, a bay, or a lake.
Sailors lean out of the boat to keep it steady. That move is called hiking.
The best scores over the races
On the sea or a lake
Field hockey
hockey
Two teams use sticks to move a small hard ball.
You may not use your feet to play the ball.
Only the flat side of the stick may be used.
A goalkeeper wears extra pads.
A goal scores one point. The ball must cross the line inside the goal.
The team with more goals wins.
On a turf pitch.
The ball is small and hard. Players wear shin guards.
On a hockey pitch
Ice hockey
Two teams skate and use sticks to move a puck.
You try to send the puck into the other goal.
A team may have six players on the ice, including the goalkeeper.
A goal scores one point.
The team with more goals when time runs out wins.
On an ice rink.
The puck is made of rubber and is frozen before a game so it slides well.
On an ice hockey rink
Figure skating
ice skating
Skaters perform a program to music.
Jumps, spins, and steps are part of the program.
You skate as a single, a pair, or a dance pair.
You must stay within the time limit.
Judges score the elements and how well they are skated.
The skater or pair with the higher score wins.
A spin can turn many times on one foot.
Judges score the program
On a figure skating rink
Skiing
alpine skiing
Skiers race down a snowy course, or perform tricks.
In a timed race you must pass every gate.
A missed gate adds a penalty or ends the run.
You get one or two runs in many races.
In a race, the clock decides. In a trick event, judges give a score.
In a race, the fastest fair time wins. In a trick event, the higher score wins.
On a snowy mountain.
Alpine skiing uses fixed-heel boots. Cross-country skiing lets the heel lift.
The fastest fair time, or a trick score
On a snowy slope
Snowboarding
Riders stand sideways on one board.
A race uses gates and a clock.
A halfpipe or slopestyle run is judged.
You must finish the course.
Races use time. Trick events use judges.
On a snow park or a mountain slope.
Both feet are fixed to the same board.
The fastest time, or a judge's score
On a snow park
Surfing
You ride a wave on a board.
Each surfer has a set time in the water.
You choose which waves to catch.
Judges watch the ride.
Judges score each wave. Your best waves are added up.
The surfer with the higher score wins the heat.
In the ocean, on a beach break or a reef.
A heat is a short timed contest between a few surfers.
Judges score the waves
In the ocean
Skateboarding
Riders perform tricks on a board with four wheels.
Street uses stairs, rails, and ledges.
Park uses bowls and ramps.
You get a set number of runs.
Judges score the tricks.
The rider with the higher score wins.
At a skate park, or on a street course.
Street and park are two different Olympic events.
Judges score the tricks
At a skate park
Climbing
sport climbing
Climbers move up a wall using holds.
Speed is a race to the top.
Boulder is a set of short problems.
Lead is a tall route on a rope.
Speed uses the clock. Boulder and lead give points for how far you climb.
In speed, the fastest climber wins. In boulder and lead, the higher score wins.
On a climbing wall, or on real rock.
A bouldering problem is short. You do it with a mat underneath, and no rope.
The fastest time, or the highest score
On a climbing wall
Weightlifting
You lift a bar with weights on each end.
The snatch is one move. The clean and jerk is two moves.
The bar must finish overhead, with arms straight.
Judges say if the lift is good.
The heaviest good lift counts. Snatch and clean and jerk are added together.
The lifter with the highest total wins.
On a lifting platform.
Lifters get three tries at each lift.
The heaviest good lifts count
On a lifting platform
Handball
team handball
Two teams of seven try to throw a ball into a goal.
You may dribble, pass, or take three steps.
Only the goalkeeper may use feet, and only in the goal area.
You may not step inside the goal area to shoot.
The ball is bigger than a football and is made to be gripped in one hand.
On a handball court
Water polo
Two teams swim and throw a ball at a goal.
You may not touch the bottom of the pool.
You pass, swim with the ball, or shoot.
A referee watches the rules from the side.
In a deep pool with floating goals.
Players wear caps so the referee can see the two teams.
In a pool with goals
Diving
You dive from a springboard or a high platform.
Each dive has a set shape in the air.
You enter the water as cleanly as you can.
Judges watch every dive.
Judges score each dive. Harder dives can earn a higher total.
The diver with the higher total wins.
At a pool with boards and platforms.
The high platform is 10 metres above the water.
Judges score each dive
At a pool with boards
Equestrian
horse riding
A rider and a horse compete as a pair.
Dressage is a test of smooth moves.
Showjumping is a course of fences.
Eventing mixes dressage, cross-country, and jumping.
Dressage uses judge scores. Showjumping counts faults for poles and for time.
In dressage, the higher score wins. In showjumping, fewer faults win.
In an arena, or on a cross-country course.
The horse and the rider are a team. Both must know the test.
A higher score, or fewer faults
In a horse arena
Triathlon
You swim, then ride a bike, then run.
You change sport in a transition area.
Your helmet must be on before you touch the bike.
The clock runs from the start of the swim to the end of the run.
First across the finish line wins.
In open water, on a bike course, and on a run course.
The Olympic order is always swim, bike, then run.
In open water, on a bike course, then a run
Netball
Two teams of seven pass a ball and try to shoot.
You may not run with the ball. You must stop when you catch it.
Each player stays in set areas of the court.
Only the goal shooter and goal attack may shoot.
On a netball court, often outdoors or in a hall.
Netball is played in many countries of the Commonwealth.
On a netball court
Kabaddi
One raider crosses into the other half.
The raider must tag a defender and get back home.
The raider chants the word kabaddi the whole time, in one breath.
Defenders try to hold the raider before the raid ends.
A tag that gets home can score a point. A stopped raid can score for the other team.
On a kabaddi court.
The raider must keep saying kabaddi without taking a new breath.
Tags can score a point
On a kabaddi court
Sumo
Two wrestlers meet in a round clay ring.
They start when both hands touch the clay.
A referee in a traditional robe watches the bout.
The bout is often very short.
There is no point score in a single bout. You win or you lose the bout.
You win if the other wrestler steps out, or if any part of them but the feet touches the clay.
In a dohyo, the clay ring, in Japan and in some other countries.
A yokozuna is the highest rank in sumo.
You win the bout, with no points
In a clay ring
Australian rules football
afl
aussie rules
Two teams of 18 move an oval ball on a huge oval.
You may kick, handball, or catch the ball.
A catch from a kick is called a mark. You may then kick freely.
Umpires watch the rules.
A goal through the middle posts is six points. A behind through the outer posts is one point.
On a large oval field in Australia.
The field is oval, not a rectangle. It is one of the biggest team pitches in sport.
A goal is six points. A behind is one.
On a big oval field
Gaelic football
gaa
Two teams of 15 play with a round ball.
You may catch, solo, or kick the ball.
You solo by dropping the ball onto your foot and back to your hands.
A goal in the net is three points. The ball over the bar is one point.
On a Gaelic pitch in Ireland, and in Irish clubs around the world.
Gaelic football and hurling are the two big Irish field games.
A goal is three points. A point is one.
On a Gaelic pitch
Curling
Teams slide heavy stones down a sheet of ice.
Sweepers brush the ice in front of the stone.
Each end, both teams throw eight stones.
You try to get stones closer to the centre than the other team.
Only the closer stones score. Each closer stone can be one point.
The team with more points after all the ends wins.
On a sheet of ice in a curling rink.
The target is called the house. The centre is the button.
Stones closer to the centre score
On a sheet of ice
Formula 1
f1
formula one
Open-wheel cars race on a closed track.
Drivers start from a grid.
They must follow flags and track limits.
A season is many races, called Grand Prix.
The first cars in a race earn points. Those points add up over the season.
The first car across the line wins that race. The driver with the most points wins the season title.
On racing tracks around the world.
A Grand Prix starts with lights. When the lights go out, the race begins.
Points for your finishing place
On a racing track
Rugby league
Two teams of 13 move an oval ball up the pitch.
You may run, pass backwards, or kick.
A team has six tackles to score before they must hand the ball over.
A try is four points. A kick through the posts after a try adds two.
On a grass pitch. The game is big in Australia, England, and the Pacific.

A try is four points
On a rugby league pitch
Softball
The pitcher throws underarm.
The ball is bigger than a baseball.
Runners move around three bases and home.
You score a run by touching every base and getting home.
The team with more runs wins.
On a softball diamond.
The pitch is underarm. In baseball the pitch is overarm.
On a softball diamond
Beach volleyball

You hit the ball over a net.
You may not catch the ball.
Wind and soft sand are part of the game.

In kata, judges watch the pattern.
A referee keeps the match fair.
In kumite, judges award points for clean scoring moves. In kata, judges score the pattern.

On a karate mat, in a dojo or a hall.
Kata means a form. You perform it alone, like a dance of set moves.
Judges award points
On a karate mat
